I looked at my younger sister, "you're the boss, whatever you tell me to do, I will do." I had a comfy chair, water and a fan in the 95 degree, humid heat. We all wore gloves and masks. We rented a dumpster. We started at 8 and quit at 5. And at dinner, no talking about the day. 3 days of hired small scale movers. We had 1 garage sale. No one was allowed in the house. We had the happiest people in the world at the garage sale. No price tags. Just a question, what do you want to pay for it? Five bucks? Fifty cents? Sold. Little kids beamed. No greater feeling. My sis and I had 3 really loud arguments, on the driveway. We made the neighbourhood buzz with gossipy happiness. And meaningful items have a home, not just a box. This leads to nights that are unbearable, even unsurvivable. That is due to combinations of temperature and humidity. In the evening, the temperature goes down but the relative humidity often increases. This is why sweat does not evaporate easily, and the body does not cool down much. 

The combination can be expressed as the wet-bulb temperature. A value of 35 C leads to heatstroke and death within a period of six hours, also for fit people. In the old climate, such values could not really happen that long because humid air is lighter and it rises. But in the near future this will happen in some city or region in the tropics: a night with mass death.

Better ventilation won't help then. For the poor, it will be almost impossible to escape. And the rich, well, probably the electrical grid will fail because of the overload from all the AC.

We went on a 3 week safari to Kenya and Tanzania this fall. It was eye opening, even through an arms-length view. KE and TZ are  magical and beautiful - gorgeous and endless vistas, lion cubs with their mom, thousands of flamingos, parades of elephants. (Google The Great Rift Valley, Amboseli park, Ngorogoro Crater.)  Three weeks of food that was all fresh, vegetables grown at many of the resorts. Even ketchup was better - no corn syrup or fillers.

Traveling between parks, we drove through towns where I spied on everyday life. I envy the simplicity of life that I saw, walking to  the open markets to buy local food and goods. However, trash is just thrown on the ground and burned in many places I saw, though I also saw efforts of cleanup in a few places. We saw plenty of shantys. When people travel, they seemingly walk for miles along a highway (no sidewalk). Or they pile into a minivan shuttle or ride 3 people on a motor bike. (I know I didn't get the complete perspective.)

A few people asked where we were from and gave us a sympathetic "oh, Trump" when we said USA. We laughed, nodded, offered our apologies. No one has ever been unkind to us, in any country, when we said were American. 

I will not take my clean tap water for granted, will recommit to fresh food and less waste, not gripe about what I pay for garbage service, not complain about traffic or road conditions. 

Thank you for this weekly newsletter. I enjoy reading it and save it for my afternoon break.

string theory implies time is illusory; i wonder if this is particularly true of love.

if time quivers in place forever, then to love someone once is to love them forever.  past loves, estranged family, even thoughtless hook-ups: a moment's love is eternal.

all one need do is vibrate like an infinitesimal string, a follicle on creation's soft underbelly.

nothing if not gullible, i take comfort in colorful strings dancing across lumpy space.  i recall, even feel, love singular, irrelevant, undiminished.  in this way i chase away loss.

[my mother, dying in a hospital bed, believes existence divides three ways: life, death & dreams.  lately she's dreaming up a storm.  dad, so good at decisions when alive, is her best advisor.  i'm a boy, glorious failure, choosing the thorniest path through life.  old now, i see strings & dreams as birds of a feather.]

My wife and I visited last fall. 
The landing at the Paro Airport is an experience in itself, as the pilot maneuvers an Airbus jet through the deep valleys of the Himalayas to complete an adrenaline filled landing, while soft music plays in the background. 
We felt transported to a medieval kingdom that balances tradition, art, nature and modern conveniences fairly well. The fortress/museum of Punakha, the suspension bridges and the monuments including the Buddha Point and Chortens are sights to behold. 
The Tiger Nest remains the crown jewel of the Bhutan tourist circuit and even here you see the seamless blend of the medieval customs and technology in the wilderness. 
As much as we heard some murmurs from the guide on young people leaving to seek a better future elsewhere (only with prodding), we saw a contended group of citizens with utmost respect for the monarchy who are proud of what this little kingdom has achieved in the last few decades!

I sincerely hope Bhutan can remain true to itself, never allowing the darker forces of unchecked capitalism and outside influence to erode what makes it so special.

Of course, people deserve to live comfortably, enjoy prosperity, and have better opportunities. There is absolutely nothing wrong with that. But please, please, don’t sell your soul in the pursuit of wealth or allow other powers to dictate your destiny.

Bhutan is a precious gem, one of the very few remaining on this planet. I hope it stays that way. The world needs places like Bhutan to remind us that there are other ways to live, grow, and find happiness between us and Mother Nature.

The idea that mass education justifies a social heirarchy based on one's degree has never been an idea universally held in the United States. This has always been a niche view of a certain elite, especially on the coasts, repulsive to many if not most Americans across the country.

It is especially repulsive when "higher education" has turned into an exploitive, rent seeking industry that demands a six figure ransom from American parents just for the chance for their children to grow up, and then does so little to ensure or meaningfully facilitate it.

Education has always offered a way. My husband and I are both educators. But let's be honest that it is not so "egalitarian." Education is heirarchical enterprise, full of fictions that rely on arbitrary human judgement as to what is "good" and "bad." It will always make one dependent on the opinion of another, easy to manipulate.

A degree can mean you learned real things, or it can mean you made your superiors happy, or your parents bribed them.

But a farmers crops either grow or don't. A factory either produces something useful or it doesn't. 

I am descended from 8 generations of successful Midwestern farmers, tradesmen, and factory owners. My husband's immigrant father became a multimillionaire owning an autobody shop.

We both have graduate degrees, and can barely pay our bills.

We are encouraging our kids to look at the trades and entrepreneurship. 

Free enterprise is the real equalizer and democratic way.

That means living in a part of the country that is not susceptible to military attack or civil violence, and hardening your current home, if possible, i.e., an adequate food supply (six weeks of MRE's and bottled water), solar power or some other independent means of electricity generation, internal and external fire suppression systems, and the traditional survival supplies that any hunter or camper might have. Instead the message is: keep calm, carry on, keep buying, keep living as you please — while the world burns.
Here's the kind of law I mean: no meat on weekends. Two meat-free days a week, for everyone. It's simple, it's fair, and meat production is one of the biggest drivers of emissions and deforestation. We already accept rules that limit our freedoms for the common good — speed limits, smoking bans. This would be no different. It's not a sacrifice; it's a weekend.
We don't need more warnings. We need governments brave enough to ask something of us.
